verdict: ENRICH now; DEFER the NEW page. Specifically: ENRICH places/singapore.md and places/hong-kong.md (each gets a short retail-tenancy / REIT-landlord section anchored on the Tier 1 primaries above, with the Bai & He paper cited only for its abstract-level framing), plus one sentence each in concepts/financialization-of-land.md and the class-monopoly-rent passage of concepts/government-granted-privileges.md, plus reciprocal See Also lines on the Anderson-series pages. DEFER research/bai-he-class-monopoly-rent-retail-financialization.md until the article body has been read. Reasons: (1) the article body was unreachable - the only paper-specific content is a ~200-word abstract, so a research page would rest on the authors' summary of findings the wiki cannot check (the wiki has accepted abstract-only pages in this series, e.g. Kyoto/Copenhagen/Oregon, graded B, but those were the only content available; here the policy facts have strong Tier 1 primaries that are worth more to a reader than a paraphrase of an abstract). (2) The paper is a critical-geography argument that names its own advocacy purpose ('debunking landlords' anti-intervention narratives and advocating for policy interventions'), so its normative conclusions are D-claims at best and must be attributed; the empirical content that can carry weight is in the official sources. (3) The official sources include material that cuts against the paper's framing (MTI 2014: no REIT effect on rents after controls; CCS 2008: no dominant landlord; CCCS 2023: market power is not itself anti-competitive and may arise from merit; HK government 2019: tenancy control has unintended consequences and the Competition Commission would not infer monopoly without location-specific evidence). A page written from the abstract alone could not present that balance honestly. (4) Upgrade path: the SAGE PDF is flagged free-to-read (bronze OA) by Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, so a human download or a browser-capable fetch will probably get the body; if it does, write NEW research/bai-he-class-monopoly-rent-retail-financialization.md (house pattern below) and link it in from at least: research/zimmerman-anderson-realpage-algorithmic-rent.md (same submarket-concentration argument), research/august-rental-financialization.md, concepts/financialization-of-land.md, places/hong-kong.md, places/singapore.md, concepts/land-monopoly.md.

SOURCE TIER (§4c): Shenjing He - Tier 1 under the rubric (University of Hong Kong, Department of Urban Planning and Design; sustained peer-reviewed output in Antipode, Economic Geography and others per the paper's own reference list, and this paper's corresponding author per Unpaywall); she is not in sources/audit/people-tiers.json, so this is a rubric judgement, not a list entry. article_abstract_verbatim_key_sentences: 'Over the past two decades, a substantial portion of retail properties in both cities has become concentrated under real estate investment trusts (REITs), a form of institutional ownership that operates under the financial imperatives.' (Abstract)

The concept of class-monopoly rent is introduced 'as a heuristic lens' and is said to be 'particularly useful for debunking landlords' anti-intervention narratives and advocating for policy interventions defending the interests of small retailers.' (Abstract)
'the monopoly power of large landlords is most evident at the submarket level rather than across an entire city, and ... small retailers face structurally unequal negotiation processes.' (Abstract)

Policy interventions highlighted: 'the development of new publicly owned marketplaces in Hong Kong and the establishment of a compulsory tenancy governance framework to promote fairer negotiations in Singapore.' (Abstract)
content_summary.what_the_abstract_does_not_say: No research design, no data, no sample, no interview count, no period beyond 'over the past two decades', no REIT-share figures, no rent figures. From the reference list alone (inference, not a finding): the article draws on Singapore parliamentary debates (PAPL 2004, 2014, 2020, 2023), LegCo papers (2019), CCCS/CCS/MTI/FTIC documents, Link REIT annual report 2013, trade and newspaper reporting (Business Times, Straits Times, SCMP, CNA, The Edge), the C&SD and DOS enterprise statistics (accessed July 2026), BIS commercial property price indices, and Bai's and Bai & He's own earlier papers - which suggests a documentary / discourse / policy-analysis design rather than a statistical one, but whether interviews were conducted cannot be told. Not to be stated as fact.
content_summary.framework_lineage: Class-monopoly rent is Harvey's (1974) Marxian concept (reference list: Harvey 1974 Regional Studies; Harvey & Chatterjee 1974 Antipode; Harvey 1985). Its recent revival in the references is largely the Anderson series already on the wiki (Anderson 2014 Geography Compass; Anderson & Arms 2023 Urban Studies; Anderson, Hansen & Scully 2022 EPA; Anderson et al. Human Geography; Revington 2021 Antipode; Teresa 2022 Geoforum; Nethercote 2024 Geoforum on UK single-family rental; Tapp & Peiser 2023 EPA 'An antitrust framework for housing'). The article also cites the critical side of the debate: Evans 1991 and Houghton 1993 (against 'monopoly rent'), Ward & Aalbers 2016 ('The shitty rent business'), Haila 1990/2000/2016 (property states).
content_summary.companion_paper: Bai & He (2025), Economic Geography 101(5-6): 411-435 (abstract only, paraphrase): revisits the 'property state' thesis for Singapore and Hong Kong, argues the rise of REITs in both cities is not a spontaneous market process but the product of established institutions - mainly privatisation and incorporation of large landholdings and, to a lesser extent, taxation policy - and proposes 'property state 2.0' as a marriage of local and financial capital. This is the better-fitting source for explaining how REITs came to hold the stock; the 2026 EPA article is about what landlords then do to small retailers.

singapore_cccs_2023: CCCS began the inquiry in April 2020 after media reports that tenants in private retail developments faced an uneven bargaining position (Exec Summary para 1-2, p.5). It examined 530 tenancy agreements (para 16, p.9) and used a tenant survey and interviews, landlord information requests and statutory powers (para 3).

Ownership: non-strata-titled private retail developments are 'typically owned by a single landlord such as a property developer or real estate investment trust' (para 5b, p.6; section IV(C) paras 15-18, p.15). At end-2019 CapitaLand Mall Trust held 14.1% of net floor space of major shopping malls (>=100,000 sq ft NLA), NTUC Enterprise 5.8%, Lendlease 4.9% (section IV(C) para 18, p.15; share figures are CCCS's). No citywide dominance - consistent with the paper's 'submarket, not citywide' point.

Market-power factors (para 7, pp.6-8): strata-titled and public (HDB) retail not viable substitutes for centrally managed malls; for chain tenants only malls in approximately the same URA planning area are substitutes; footfall, MRT-station location and mall management matter; switching costs are high (leases up to three years; fit-out capex); limited alternative space. CCCS conclusion (para 13, p.9): some developments 'may possess some degree of market power within a planning area.' Evidence: median retail rents higher in suburban regions than the Central Region, Q1 2015-Q1 2020 (para 9, p.8; section VII(A) para 62, p.32); the highest revenue-per-sq-ft malls are 'typically the largest or the only retail developments in their respective planning areas and ... next to the main MRT station' (para 10, p.8); footfall and mall management are statistically significant in a regression on gross revenue per sq ft (para 11; Annex 3).

Bargaining: tenants 'often found themselves with little bargaining power', with a 'take-it-or-leave-it' landlord attitude and no transparent rent benchmark (para 12, pp.8-9). Clauses landlords can dictate include pre-termination for asset-enhancement works without compensation.

Caveat in the Commission's own words (para 2, p.5): 'It is not anti-competitive for a landlord to possess market power or to be able to charge higher rents or be more profitable.' Landlords may have market power 'based on competitive merits'.

Anti-competitive clauses: only 18 of 530 agreements had exclusivity-radius clauses, assessed as not significant (para 16, p.9); widespread landlord-designated electricity retailer clauses with mark-ups were the competition concern (paras 17-20, p.9-10). CCCS recommended an industry-wide solution and noted the Code of Conduct incorporates it (paras 21-22, 93 / pp.10-11, 44).

Timeline (Exec Summary para 4, pp.5-6; confirmed on ftic.org.sg/about): Fair Tenancy Pro Tem Committee formed 26 June 2020; Code of Conduct introduced 26 March 2021; Fair Tenancy Industry Committee set up 3 May 2021 as custodian of the Code.
singapore_statute_and_code: Lease Agreements for Retail Premises Act 2023 (No. 28 of 2023): passed by Parliament 3 August 2023, assented to 21 August 2023, gazetted 8 September 2023 (Acts Supplement No. 32). Long title: 'to establish the Fair Tenancy Industry Committee, the terms on which retail premises may be leased, the resolution of disputes concerning those terms'. Commencement is by ministerial notification (s.1); the commencement date was NOT found in the fetched text. Parts: 2 Fair Tenancy Industry Committee; 3 Code of Conduct; 4 Dispute Resolution (complaints, authorised dispute resolution bodies, mediation, adjudication, enforcement). 'Qualifying lease' = lease of retail premises meeting the First Schedule minimum period, signed after commencement of Part 3 (s.2). The Act refers to 'permitted deviations' declared jointly by landlord and tenant.

Code of Conduct, 3rd edition dated 1 Nov 2023: effective from 1 February 2024; applies to qualifying leases signed on or after that date with a period of one year or more (Intro and para 3.1.1, pp.1-2); to be read with the Act, which prevails on inconsistency. Part A good-faith negotiation principles; Part B eleven leasing principles on key tenancy terms; Part C confidentiality and data transparency; Part D dispute resolution. Examples of Part B content: exclusivity clauses 'must not be included' except by joint agreement with a declaration filed with FTIC within 14 days or the clause is void (Part B para 1.1-1.3, pp.7-8); landlord may pre-terminate for redevelopment only if it carries out substantial works needing vacant possession, with at least 6 months' notice and tenant compensation, and not 'purely for the purposes of changing the tenant mix' (para 4.1-4.2, p.13); rental formula must not be an 'either/or, whichever is higher' structure and must be a single computation across the term (para 11.1, p.20). A search of the Code text found no rent cap or limit on rent increases: it governs terms, process and disputes, not rent levels - the wiki should not describe it as rent control.
singapore_earlier_official_studies_count: CCS (2008) market study (consultant DTZ; CCS views): of an estimated 2.03 million sq m of private non-strata retail space, developers owned about 64%, REITs about 29%, private equity funds 7%; only CapitaLand Mall Trust (14%) and Mapletree Investments (6%) exceeded 5% (para 17, p.10). Retailers 'usually do not have much bargaining power' on terms, though power 'tended to be stronger in non REIT/property fund malls' (para 23). REITs 'have very specific revenue targets set quarterly and annually, e.g., 3-4% annual rental growth' and rent is 'often the over-riding factor in malls owned by REITs' (paras 22, 32). CCS's own view (para 38(a), p.16): 'No landlord is likely to hold a dominant position in retail malls', and 'unlikely to be competition concerns in the retail mall rental market at this juncture'; para 38(d) credits REIT entry with improved mall management. Note the 2008 study predates the 2020-23 CCCS inquiry, which reached a more qualified, planning-area-level conclusion.

MTI (2014), 35 REIT-owned and 76 single-owner malls, 2000-2013, IRAS rental-transaction microdata: REIT malls' rents grew faster in raw terms (20% CAGR 2009-2013 vs 9.2% for single-owner malls), but 'after controlling for the observable characteristics of the malls such as location and the asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs) taken, we find that the rents in REIT-owned malls are not statistically different from rents in single-owner malls', and 'no evidence' that rents rose as a result of REIT acquisition (Executive Summary, p.22). The paper carries a disclaimer that the views are the authors' own. This is the strongest official statement of the 'REITs don't raise rents' position the Bai & He abstract calls an 'anti-intervention narrative'.
hong_kong_thb_legco_2019: The Housing Authority divested 180 properties in 2005 through The Link Real Estate Investment Trust (now Link REIT), 'including retail and carparking facilities', to focus on core subsidised housing and improve its finances; the efficiency of the commercial facilities was expected to improve under private commercial operation (para 8, p.4). The Court of Final Appeal in 2005 held the divestment consistent with s.4(1) of the Housing Ordinance and that public rental tenants had no statutory right to HA's continued retention and control of the facilities (para 9, p.4); divested properties remain subject to land-lease conditions and HA covenants, including concessionary lettings for social welfare facilities (para 10).

The Ip/Mak members' bill ('Regulation of Commercial Facilities in Public and Subsidized Housing (Legislative Provisions) Bill') would have introduced a cap mechanism on rent increases, a right of first refusal to renew leases and a vacancy tax on 147 divested properties (paras 1, 13). The Government did not support it (para 21): Basic Law Art.74 (members' bills), Arts.6 and 105 (property rights, proportionality), free-market and pro-competition commitments, and the view that tenancy control tends to produce unintended consequences (para 15, quoting the 2014 Long Term Housing Strategy on residential tenancy control) - e.g. owners favouring chain stores, lower maintenance incentive, higher miscellaneous fees.

Competition Commission view relayed in para 12 (p.5): 'it would be difficult to conclude whether an owner 'monopolises' a market without looking into the actual market conditions of specific locations' - i.e. the regulator itself frames monopoly as location-specific, which is close to the paper's submarket point, though the Commission draws the opposite policy conclusion.

Community views recorded (para 18, p.7): supporters said rent increases at divested properties had been notably higher than the average rate for all shop premises and forced small shops out; the paper reports this as opinion, not as measured fact - no rent series is given in the THB paper.

Hong Kong's 'publicly owned marketplaces' response: the Government said it was 'gearing up the preparation work for a number of new public market development projects' and would 'go full steam ahead', with provision assessed case-by-case under the Hong Kong Planning Standards and Guidelines (para 23, p.9). Later project-specific records (specific new markets, dates, stall counts) were not located and the paper's own account of them is unread.

existing_wiki_coverage.hong_kong_and_singapore_places_pages: places/hong-kong.md (reviewed 2026-07-26) and places/singapore.md (reviewed 2026-07-18) are about state land leasing, land premiums (HK ~13-24% of revenue), MTR Rail+Property, HDB, and Singapore's congestion pricing. Neither mentions REITs, retail landlords, or tenancy regulation. There is a built-in tension worth stating: both are the wiki's 'public landlordship' showcase cases, yet in both the state has moved retail assets into REIT hands (HK: HA's 2005 Link divestment of 180 properties; Singapore: REIT/developer-owned malls) and the location rent on retail space is collected by private landlords, while the state's capture is the lump-sum premium at grant. That is interpretive (D) and should be labelled as analysis if used.
existing_wiki_coverage.class_monopoly_rent_series: Five pages use the concept: research/anderson-kyoto-cultural-monopoly-rent.md (cultural monopoly rent, Kyoto; abstract + references, B), research/anderson-dascher-copenhagen-land-rent.md (state monopoly rent; abstract, B), research/anderson-landlord-rent-control-class-monopoly.md (Oregon SB 608 landlord rhetoric; abstract, B), research/zimmerman-anderson-realpage-algorithmic-rent.md (full text, A; neighbourhood-level concentration: 70% of apartments run by 10 managers in Belltown/South Lake Union, ~90% of large DC multifamily RealPage-priced), and concepts/government-granted-privileges.md (one paragraph on Melgaco 2026, 'Rent Seeking and the City: Urban Screens', abstract-level A for the abstract). The Anderson pages cross-link each other (a four-page ring) and each states that class monopoly rent is a Marxian/critical-geography concept distinct from Georgist land rent. Closest conceptual neighbour to Bai & He: Zimmerman & Anderson (submarket concentration vs national share) and the Oregon paper (landlord anti-intervention rhetoric). Karp (research/karp-landlord-private-government.md) is the political-theory 'domination' counterpart and says financialization/REIT structure is covered elsewhere.
existing_wiki_coverage.financialization_pages: concepts/financialization-of-land.md (reviewed 2026-07-26) is credit/mortgage-led plus August (Canada), NEF and Lacerda & Fiorentino (Brazil); it has no commercial-property or Asian case. research/august-rental-financialization.md covers REITs and financialized residential landlords in Canada (REITs 0 to ~10% of apartment suites 1996-2017), with Harvey's 'accumulation by dispossession'; it is residential only. uncertainties: Article body unread: research design, case selection, time span, data, interview count, the specific REIT-share and rent figures, the exact Hong Kong marketplace interventions it analyses, and its treatment of the Singapore Act are all unknown. Everything attributed to the paper rests on the Crossref/Semantic Scholar abstract (identical in both) and an inference from its reference list.

The abstract's two policy examples are described at a high level; the Hong Kong 'new publicly owned marketplaces' could refer to Government public-market projects (THB 2019 para 23) or to a different programme (e.g. HA-run or district markets). Not resolved from the abstract. Do not name specific markets until the body is read.

Singapore Act: only s.1-2 and the Part headings were read; the commencement date, the First Schedule minimum lease period, the Second Schedule list of retail premises, the enforcement powers and any penalties were not. The Code says qualifying leases are those of one year or more and signed on or after 1 Feb 2024; the Act's own commencement notification was not located.

Whether the Code covers all landlords or is limited by the Second Schedule premises list was not checked. The abstract's phrase 'compulsory tenancy governance framework' is the authors' description; the Code is described by FTIC as industry-led and by the Act as statutory - the 'compulsory' status rests on the Act (Part 3), which is unread beyond its table of contents.
The CCS 2008 conclusion (para 38) is a 2008 market-wide view based on consultant DTZ's data; it was superseded in emphasis, not formally withdrawn, by the 2023 inquiry's planning-area analysis.

MTI 2014 is dated and pre-pandemic; the CCCS 2023 inquiry used 2015-2020 rent data. No official post-2020 rent series for Singapore retail or for Link REIT shops was obtained; none of the primaries measures the rent effect of the 2024 Code.

Hong Kong: the THB 2019 paper is the Government's position paper, a Tier 1 source for what the Government said and decided but an interested party on the merits. It reports the 'rents rose faster than average' claim only as community opinion; no Hong Kong rent series or Link REIT market-share figure was fetched. The Link REIT 2005 IPO terms, the 2013 annual report figures cited by the article and the Rating and Valuation Department retail rent indices are unread.

Author tiers: Shenjing He's Tier 1 standing is a rubric judgement from affiliation, publication venues in the reference list and the corresponding-author flag; OpenAlex's profile for her ORCID is fragmentary (2 works) and could not be used to confirm output. Bai's standing is limited as described under claim_grade. Neither is in people-tiers.json; T1 may wish to add them with these notes.

Wiki-internal inconsistency spotted while cross-checking: this article's reference list cites the Oregon paper as 'Anderson, Zickefoose, Andrie et al. (2025), Human Geography 18(1): 46-58', whereas research/anderson-landlord-rent-control-class-monopoly.md gives 2024 (volume 18 issue 1 would normally be a 2025 issue, though the DOI suffix 241234546 indicates a 2024 submission; the wiki's frontmatter year and title say 2024). The page's own 'Sources' says 'the published bibliographic record' was followed. T1 should check Crossref for the issue date and align title/year.

Normative stance: the authors are explicitly advocating intervention; the scanner note's phrase 'policy responses ... defend small retailers' repeats the authors' own framing and should not become wiki voice. Georgist relevance is indirect: class-monopoly rent is Harvey's Marxian concept, and the wiki's own pages stress the distinction. Any Georgist reading (that these are cases where publicly created location value is captured by private landlords at the flow level while the state captures it only at grant) is an interpretation (D) and needs to be labelled as analysis.
